      Warm-up

      Vibrating glass: warm-up

      2 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 174

      Answer

      Adding water generally lowers the pitch of a rubbed glass. The moving water adds inertia to the vibration, so the resonant frequency decreases. Compare the same glass at different fill levels.

      Question 2Textbook p. 174

      Answer

      Yes. A damp finger rubbing the rim can excite the glass itself. The vibrating glass sends sound waves through the air even when the glass is empty.

      Quick check

      Frequency and period: quick check

      3 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 176

      Answer

      1. f = N/Δt = 50.0/40.0 = 1.25 Hz.
      2. T = 1/f = 1/1.25 = 0.800 s.
      Question 2Textbook p. 176

      Answer

      1. f = 7680/30 = 256 Hz.
      2. T = 1/256 = 3.91 × 10⁻³ s.
      Question 3Textbook p. 176

      Answer

      One complete back-and-forth cycle takes 4.0 s. f = 1/T = 1/4.0 = 0.25 Hz.

      Question 6.1.1Textbook p. 177

      Answer

      v = fλ = (256 Hz)(1.29 m) = 330.24 m/s ≈ 330 m/s.

      Practice

      Practice 6.1.1: calculating wave speed

      3 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 178

      Answer

      1. At fixed speed, λ = v/f. Doubling f halves λ.
      2. Halving f doubles λ.
      Question 2Textbook p. 178

      Answer

      f = v/λ = (340 m/s)/(1.70 m) = 200 Hz.

      Question 3Textbook p. 178

      Answer

      λ = v/f = (3.0 m/s)/(2.0 Hz) = 1.5 m.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-1A: waves in springs

      6 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 179

      Answer

      Use your travel times over a known length. Compute v = distance/time for each spring and compare. Transverse speed increases with tension and decreases with mass per stretched metre. Diameter alone does not determine which spring is faster.

      Question 2Textbook p. 179

      Answer

      Compare the travel times of a compression pulse over the same distance, or calculate distance/time for each spring. Longitudinal speed depends on the spring’s effective stiffness and inertia. Use your observations to rank the two springs.

      Question 3Textbook p. 179

      Answer

      For small pulses at the same tension and stretch, speed is approximately independent of amplitude. Compare travel times. A very large pulse can alter the stretch and tension.

      Question 4Textbook p. 179

      Answer

      Greater tension generally gives a faster transverse pulse. For an ideal stretched string, v = √(F/μ), where μ is the mass per unit length. Stretching the spring may change μ as well as the tension.

      Question 5Textbook p. 179

      Answer

      The disturbance propagates. Each coil moves temporarily about its equilibrium position as the pulse passes. Track one marked coil to separate local motion from pulse motion.

      Question 6Textbook p. 179

      Answer

      At a fixed end the transverse pulse inverts. A crest returns as a trough. At the boundary, the incoming and reflected displacements sum to zero.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-1B: waves in a tank

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 180

      Answer

      In still water of uniform depth, a point pulse spreads at the same speed in every direction. A circular front stays centred on the source, so its radius is the same in every direction at a given time.

      Question 2Textbook p. 180

      Answer

      Increasing f usually reduces the wavelength in this tank. Compare crest spacing for the same depth. The relation is λ = v/f. Exact inverse proportionality assumes the speed stays constant.

      Section review

      6.1 Review: wave properties

      12 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      A disturbance starts a wave. A single disturbance can launch a pulse. Repeated vibrations of the source generate a periodic wave.

      Question 2Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      The intended comparison is a single pulse, which has no repetition frequency and no periodic wavelength. A pulse does have an amplitude. A displacement amplitude of zero everywhere means there is no disturbance.

      Question 3Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      107.3 MHz = 1.073 × 10⁸ Hz, or 107.3 million oscillations per second.

      Question 4Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      T = 1/f = 1/(25 Hz) = 0.040 s.

      Question 5Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      f = 1/T = 1/(2.0 s) = 0.50 Hz.

      Question 6Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      If 8 m describes the full trough-to-crest height, the amplitude is approximately 4 m. Amplitude is measured from equilibrium to a crest or trough.

      Question 7Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      One revolution takes 60 s. f = 1/60 s = 0.0167 Hz.

      Question 8Textbook p. 181

      Answer

      One revolution takes 12 h = 43 200 s. f = 1/43 200 s = 2.31 × 10⁻⁵ Hz.

      Question 9Textbook p. 182

      Answer

      T = 1/f. Tripling the frequency makes the period one-third of its original value.

      Question 10Textbook p. 182

      Answer

      f = v/λ = (25 cm/s)/(2.5 cm) = 10 Hz. The centimetres cancel.

      Question 11Textbook p. 182

      Answer

      λ = c/f = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(3.0 × 10¹⁰) = 1.0 × 10⁻² m = 1.0 cm.

      Question 12Textbook p. 182

      Answer

      Successive crests arrive 6 s apart, so T = 6 s. v = λ/T ≈ 12/6 = 2 m/s.

      Warm-up

      Overlapping ripples: warm-up

      1 entries

      Question Warm-upTextbook p. 183

      Answer

      Draw concentric crests around each splash. Mark X at intersections of two crest circles, where the upward displacements add. For simultaneous identical splashes, locations equally distant from both sources receive matching parts of the two ripples at the same time.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 1: circular-wave reflection

      1 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question ConclusionTextbook p. 189

      Answer

      A rigid, lossless barrier that transmits no energy can reflect all incident energy in an ideal model. A real barrier can absorb, transmit, or scatter some energy, and a finite barrier lets waves pass around its ends. Reflected circular fronts appear to come from the mirror-image source behind a flat barrier.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 2: straight-wave reflection

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 189

      Answer

      θᵢ = θᵣ. Measure both ray angles from the normal. The angles between the wavefronts and the barrier are equal as well.

      Question 2Textbook p. 189

      Answer

      The reflected waves remain in the same water at the same depth. Their speed, frequency, and wavelength stay the same in the ideal model. Amplitude can decrease.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 3: curved reflectors

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 190

      Answer

      Plane waves arriving along the axis reflect and converge toward the focus. A parabolic reflector can concentrate wave energy near that point.

      Question 2Textbook p. 190

      Answer

      Waves spreading from the focus leave the ideal reflector as approximately straight, parallel wavefronts travelling along the axis. This reverses the focusing process.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 4: water-wave refraction

      6 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 191

      Answer

      In the ripple-tank model the waves slow down in shallower water, as shown by closer crest spacing at the same frequency.

      Question 2Textbook p. 191

      Answer

      Use v = fλ and constant f. The ratio v(shallow)/v(deep) = λ(shallow)/λ(deep). Measure several crest spacings in each region and divide by the number of intervals before taking the ratio.

      Question 3Textbook p. 191

      Answer

      The generator fixes the number of crests per second. At a stationary boundary each incident cycle drives one transmitted cycle, so the frequency stays constant.

      Question 4Textbook p. 191

      Answer

      If the fronts are parallel to the boundary, the direction of travel is along the normal. The waves continue straight while slowing and shortening their wavelength.

      Question 5Textbook p. 191

      Answer

      At oblique incidence the ray bends toward the normal as it enters slower, shallow water. The refraction angle is smaller than the incidence angle. Equivalently, the transmitted crests make a smaller angle to the boundary.

      Question 6Textbook p. 191

      Answer

      On returning to faster deep water, the ray bends away from the normal. If the two boundaries are parallel and the outer depths match, the final ray is parallel to the original. The exit refraction angle then equals the original incidence angle.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 5: diffraction

      5 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 192

      Answer

      For a fixed gap or obstacle, diffraction is more noticeable with longer wavelengths. Compare wavelength with the size of the feature.

      Question 2Textbook p. 192

      Answer

      For fixed wavelength, smaller openings give broader spreading when the opening is comparable to or smaller than λ. A very small opening can transmit less energy.

      Question 3Textbook p. 192

      Answer

      Draw nearly semicircular wavefronts centred on the opening. The gap acts roughly like a point source when it is narrow compared with the wavelength.

      Question 4Textbook p. 192

      Answer

      1. If the obstacle is very small relative to λ, the wave wraps around it with little persistent shadow.
      2. If its width is comparable to λ, the fronts curve appreciably around both edges.
      3. If the obstacle is much larger than λ, a clear shadow forms behind it, with some spreading at the edges.
      Question 5Textbook p. 192

      Answer

      Examples include hearing someone around a corner, seeing ripples spread around a pier, and seeing a starburst when viewing a streetlight through fine mesh.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 6A: spring interference

      2 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 193

      Answer

      The displacements add. Equal crests of height A give a combined crest of 2A during exact overlap.

      Question 2Textbook p. 193

      Answer

      Equal and opposite displacements add to zero where they coincide. The original pulses continue after they pass through each other.

      Investigation

      Investigation 6-2, Station 6B: water-wave interference

      4 entries

      Investigation procedure and data tables
      Question 1Textbook p. 193

      Answer

      For equal amplitudes, a crest and trough cancel. The screen loses the alternating bright/dark crest pattern there, leaving a relatively steady region or nodal line.

      Question 2Textbook p. 193

      Answer

      Crests add to crests, and troughs add to troughs. The displacement is larger and the projected pattern shows stronger variation at this maximum.

      Question 3Textbook p. 193

      Answer

      The second distance must be a half-integer multiple of λ, such as (n ± ½)λ. In general the absolute path difference is (m + ½)λ for m = 0, 1, 2, …. Several distances are possible if the geometry allows them.

      Question 4Textbook p. 193

      Answer

      The second distance can be any integer multiple of λ allowed by the geometry, including mλ itself. The path difference must be an integer multiple of λ, including zero.

      Section review

      6.2 Review: wave phenomena

      11 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 194

      Answer

      Reflection. Put a virtual source the same distance behind the barrier as the real source is in front. Draw reflected circular arcs on the incident side of the barrier, centred on that virtual source.

      Question 2Textbook p. 194

      Answer

      Diffraction. Leave the straight incident fronts on the left. Draw spreading semicircular fronts centred on the narrow gap on the right.

      Question 3Textbook p. 194

      Answer

      Diffraction. The closely spaced threads act like a two-dimensional grating, spreading light into directions that can produce the starburst pattern.

      Question 4Textbook p. 194

      Answer

      1. Refraction at each boundary.
      2. In shallow water the crest spacing is smaller, so λ and v decrease at fixed f. The fronts turn. At the parallel exit boundary they turn back to their original orientation if the two deep-water speeds are equal.
      Question 5Textbook p. 194

      Answer

      1. No. Like-signed equal pulses add.
      2. No. The pulses have the same sign and unequal amplitudes.
      3. Yes. Mark the midpoint where the centres meet. Equal and opposite profiles sum to zero at exact overlap.
      4. No. Opposite signs alone are insufficient because the amplitudes differ.
      5. No. The two lobes arrive in opposite spatial order, so the profiles cannot cancel everywhere simultaneously.
      6. Yes. Mark the overlap location. The tall crest aligns with the deep trough and the shorter crest aligns with the shallower trough.
      Question 6Textbook p. 195

      Answer

      All three can interfere. Sound pressure, the electric field of light, and water-surface displacement can each superpose.

      Question 7Textbook p. 195

      Answer

      All three can exhibit a Doppler shift in measured frequency when source and observer move relative to each other along the line of travel. For waves in a medium, source and observer motion are measured relative to the medium.

      Question 8Textbook p. 195

      Answer

      Yes. Moving toward a stationary source makes you encounter the wavefronts more often. Moving away makes you encounter them less often.

      Question 9Textbook p. 195

      Answer

      The aircraft was supersonic when it generated the shock that reached you. The shock travels outward and can reach the ground after the aircraft has passed.

      Question 10Textbook p. 195

      Answer

      The sound barrier refers to the aerodynamic effects near Mach 1, including compression and shock formation. A sonic boom is the sound heard when a shock from supersonic motion passes an observer.

      Question 11Textbook p. 195

      Answer

      Chapter review

      Chapter 6 Review Questions

      15 entries

      Question 1Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      A pulse is a single travelling disturbance. A periodic wave repeats regularly in time because the source repeats its motion.

      Question 2Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      1. A crest is a point of maximum upward displacement.
      2. A trough is a point of maximum downward displacement.
      3. Wavelength is the distance between successive points at the same phase, such as crest to crest.
      4. Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second at a point.
      5. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.
      Question 3Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      1 Hz = one cycle per second = 1 s⁻¹.

      Question 4Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      Frequency and period are reciprocals. f = 1/T and T = 1/f.

      Question 5Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      1. f = 50/20 = 2.5 Hz.
      2. T = 1/2.5 = 0.40 s.
      Question 6Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      For a transverse wave, the oscillation is perpendicular to the wave’s travel direction. For a longitudinal wave, it is parallel.

      Question 7Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      v = fλ. A crest travels one wavelength in one period, so v = λ/T.

      Question 8Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      λ = c/f = (3.0 × 10⁸)/60 = 5.0 × 10⁶ m, or about 5000 km.

      Question 9Textbook p. 196

      Answer

      λ = v/f = 330/512 ≈ 0.645 m (about 0.64 m).

      Question 11Textbook p. 197

      Answer

      Refraction is a change in direction as wave speed changes, as when an oblique light ray enters water. Diffraction is spreading around edges or through an opening, as when you hear a voice around a corner.

      Question 12Textbook p. 197

      Answer

      1. The wavelength decreases because λ = v/f.
      2. The frequency stays the same at a stationary boundary.
      3. At oblique incidence the slower wave bends toward the normal.
      4. At normal incidence the propagation direction is unchanged.
      Question 13Textbook p. 197

      Answer

      1. Constructive interference occurs when displacements reinforce, such as two crests meeting.
      2. Destructive interference occurs when opposite displacements reduce the sum. Equal and opposite displacements cancel completely.
      Question 14Textbook p. 197

      Answer

      For two coherent, in-phase sources of equal amplitude, a nodal line forms where the path difference is (m + ½)λ. A maximum occurs where the difference is mλ, including zero. Here m is a nonnegative integer.

      Question 15Textbook p. 197

      Answer

      The first mirror sends radiation from its focus into a nearly parallel beam. The facing mirror collects that beam and concentrates it at its focus, where the match absorbs energy.

      Question 16Textbook p. 197

      Answer

      v = fλ = (2.2 × 10⁶)(5.10 × 10⁻⁴) = 1122 m/s. The pulse travels down and back, so depth = vΔt/2 = (1122)(8.0)/2 ≈ 4.5 × 10³ m, measured below the submarine.

      Question 1Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      Label a highest point crest and a lowest point trough. Mark amplitude vertically from the midline to a crest. Mark wavelength horizontally between adjacent crests or adjacent troughs.

      A is half the trough-to-crest height. A = 4.2/2 = 2.1 m.

      Question 3Textbook p. 198

      λ = v/f = (3.4 × 10²)/256 ≈ 1.3 m.

      Question 4Textbook p. 198

      610 nm = 6.10 × 10⁻⁷ m. f = c/λ = (3.00 × 10⁸)/(6.10 × 10⁻⁷) = 4.92 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

      Question 5Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      f = 3 Hz and v = 4 m/s. λ = v/f = 4/3 ≈ 1.3 m.

      Question 6Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      1. f = 1/(100 s) = 0.010 Hz.
      2. f = 1/(0.5 s) = 2 Hz.
      3. f = 1/(1.0 × 10⁻² s) = 1.0 × 10² Hz.
      Question 7Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      1. Wave 1 has the longest period.
      2. Wave 1 has the lowest frequency.
      3. Wave 4 has the highest frequency.

      These comparisons assume the diagrams use a common time axis or show spatial snapshots of waves travelling at the same speed. Spatial spacing by itself gives wavelength.

      Question 8Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      One revolution takes 12 h = 43 200 s.

      Question 9Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      One revolution takes 60 s.

      Question 10Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      1. 3.00 min = 180 s. f = 36/180 = 0.200 Hz.
      2. T = 1/f = 5.00 s.
      Question 11Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      The spider returns to the needle’s position after one revolution. T = (60 s)/33 ≈ 1.8 s.

      Question 12Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      Wavelength decreases when the source frequency increases, assuming the same wave speed. If speed is approximately constant, λ is inversely proportional to f.

      Question 13Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      λ = v/f = 2.5/34 ≈ 0.074 m = 7.4 cm.

      Question 14Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      25 cm = 0.25 m and 5 km/h = 5/3.6 m/s ≈ 1.39 m/s. f = 1.39/0.25 ≈ 5.6 Hz before rounding to the precision of the given speed.

      Question 15Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      v = fλ = (200)(35) = 7.0 × 10³ m/s from the given data. This is far above the speed of sound in room-temperature air.

      Question 16Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      Using 250 wavelengths across 100 m gives λ ≈ 100/250 = 0.40 m. If 100 m is measured from the first crest to the 250th crest, use 249 intervals and get 0.402 m, which also rounds to 0.40 m.

      Question 17Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      600 nm = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m. f = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(6.00 × 10⁻⁷) = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. A wavelength of 600 nm is approximately orange.

      Question 18Textbook p. 198

      Answer

      Frequency stays the same across a stationary boundary, so the period also stays the same. Speed, wavelength, and amplitude can change.
